newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MANDELA HONOURS COMPOSER OF NKOSI SIKELEL IAFRIKA.
newsitem.headline: MANDELA HONOURS COMPOSER OF NKOSI SIKELEL IAFRIKA.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela on Tuesday unveiled a monument to the composer of the hymn that is the national anthem of three African states, calling it the torch that lit South Africa's path to freedom.
The ceremony at a Johannesburg cemetery, staged on the Heritage Day national holiday, honoured Enoch Sontonga who composed Nkosi Sikelel iAfrika (God Bless Africa) in 1897.

The music and lyrics were adopted by Mandela's African National Congress as its official hymn at its inaugural meeting in 1912 and became the main theme of South Africa's national anthem after historic all-race elections in 1994.
Political prisoners on death row sang the hymn on the eve of executions before a moratorium on hangings was instituted in 1990.

Sontonga's unmarked grave was discovered only in April after a search of about 18 months. The entry in the cemetery register when Sontonga was buried in 1905 read: "Enoch, 32 years, April 19, Kaffir." Kaffir is a pejorative term for blacks.
"The circumstances of Sontonga's burial, in a segregated cemetery, in an unmarked grave, is a harsh reminder of the times in which the hymn was composed," Mandela said in a speech at the ceremony.

"We owe (this ceremony) to the countless men, women and children across the generations who carried this anthem in their hearts, in the face of bullets and the hangman's noose; in moments of terrible privation and in the joy of celebration," Mandela said.
The tune is the basis of the national anthems of Zambia and Tanzania. Zimbabwe also used it as an anthem until two years ago.
"Nkosi Sikelel iAfrika is a prayer for crops and rain, for harvest, health and peace for all," Mandela said. "It is the torch that has lit our way."

Mandela said Heritage Day, an annual holiday declared by his government after it won the 1994 election, was intended to honour those who had fought injustice and inequity so the country could "rise like the phoenix from the ashes of division and conflict."
In a separate Heritage Day ceremony in the Zulu heartland province of KwaZulu-Natal, Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini urged South Africans to put their differences aside.
"Let us stop making ourselves the scorn of other nations," the king, clad in traditional leopard skin regalia, told a ululating crowd of about 3,000 people in the Indian Ocean port city of Durban.
KwaZulu-Natal has been the scene of the worst of the political violence in which more than 20,000 people have been killed in South Africa since the mid-1980s.
The violence, which has eased since the 1994 election, pitted the ANC against the Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party and members of the white-led security forces.
